body:
What makes glass different from a crystal?

Glass is generally a hard, brittle, amorphous solid. An amorphous solid lacks the long-range regular arrangement of atoms characteristic of a crystalline solid.

In an ordinary crystal, the arrangement of particles repeats in an orderly pattern. In glass, the atomic network is disordered over long distances. This structural distinction explains why glass is classified as non-crystalline.

Glass is a solid at room temperature. Describing ordinary glass as a liquid slowly flowing in windows is misleading. Its amorphous structure does not make it an ordinary liquid.

Raw materials for ordinary glass

The most common commercial glass is soda-lime glass. Its main glass-forming ingredient is silica, chemically silicon dioxide, SiO2, usually supplied by suitable sand.

Other raw materials modify how the glass is made and how it performs:

  • Silica: Forms the main glass network.
  • Soda ash: Sodium carbonate, Na2CO3, helps lower the temperature required for practical glass processing.
  • Limestone: Calcium carbonate, CaCO3, supplies lime, which helps improve chemical durability.

Recycled crushed glass, called cullet, can also be included in glass manufacture. Suitable cullet reduces the need for new raw materials and can lower the energy required for melting.

Common types of glass

TypeCharacteristicCommon application
Soda-lime glassCommon, economical general-purpose glassWindow panes, bottles and jars
Borosilicate glassGreater resistance to rapid temperature changes than ordinary soda-lime glassSuitable laboratory ware and heat-resistant household articles

Borosilicate glass contains boron-containing components in addition to silica. Its composition gives it relatively low thermal expansion, helping it resist thermal shock. Greater heat resistance does not mean that borosilicate glass is unbreakable.

Why glass is useful

Many glasses are transparent, allowing visible light to pass through them. Glass can also be coloured, moulded into containers and made into sheets. It is resistant to many common chemicals and does not corrode like iron.

These properties explain its use in windows, bottles, drinking vessels, laboratory equipment and optical products. However, glass can fracture under impact, and its chemical resistance is not unlimited.

Glass and plastic: an important comparison

Glass and plastic can both be used for bottles and containers, but they are different classes of materials. Ordinary glass is an inorganic amorphous solid, while common plastics are organic polymers. Glass is generally more brittle and often heavier; plastic is commonly lighter and can be more flexible.

Glass can be recycled by remelting suitable collected material. Correct sorting matters: different glass compositions may not be compatible with the same recycling process. Recyclability therefore does not mean that every glass article belongs in the same collection stream.

Prelims focus

  • Ordinary glass is an amorphous, non-crystalline solid.
  • Silica is silicon dioxide, SiO2.
  • Soda-lime glass is commonly used for windows and bottles.
  • Soda ash is sodium carbonate, Na2CO3.
  • Limestone supplies lime and helps improve glass durability.
  • Borosilicate glass is valued for resistance to thermal shock.
  • Trap: Amorphous glass should not be classified as an ordinary liquid at room temperature.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, ch. 4, Sorting Materials into Groups, printed pp. 26–30, 2018–19 edition. Corning Museum of Glass, glassmaking materials and techniques, consulted 3 November 2026. University of New South Wales, School of Materials Science and Engineering, introductory information on glass composition and amorphous structure, consulted 3 November 2026. Glass Packaging Institute, glass ingredients and recycling information, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Glass: Composition, Structure, Properties and Applications

body:
Why are household chemicals important?

Many familiar household products contain compounds whose chemical properties make them useful for cooking, cleaning, washing or hygiene. Their everyday names can be confusing because compounds with similar names may have different formulas and applications.

Common substances and their chemical identities

Common nameChemical identityImportant use or property
Common saltSodium chloride, NaClFood seasoning and chemical raw material
Baking sodaSodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3Mildly basic; releases CO2 when reacting with suitable acids
Washing sodaSodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2OCleaning and softening hard water
VinegarDilute aqueous ethanoic acid, CH3COOHAcidic food ingredient
Bleaching powderTraditionally represented by CaOCl2Bleaching and disinfection applications
Household liquid bleachUsually contains sodium hypochlorite, NaOClBleaching and surface disinfection when properly used

Baking soda and washing soda are different compounds. Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate. Washing soda is hydrated sodium carbonate. Their alkalinity and suitable uses differ.

Similarly, bleaching powder and liquid household bleach are not identical products. The simplified formula CaOCl2 is commonly used for bleaching powder in school chemistry, but commercial bleaching-powder formulations are more complex than a single perfectly pure compound. Liquid bleach usually contains sodium hypochlorite in water.

How does soap remove grease?

Soap commonly consists of sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids. A soap molecule has 2 functionally different parts:

  • A hydrophilic part that interacts with water.
  • A hydrophobic hydrocarbon part that associates with oils and grease.

In water, soap molecules can gather around small grease droplets to form structures called micelles. Their hydrophobic parts point towards the grease, while their hydrophilic parts face the surrounding water. Agitation and rinsing then help carry away the dispersed grease.

Soap versus synthetic detergent

Both soaps and synthetic detergents contain substances that help water remove oily dirt. However, their chemical structures differ.

Hard water contains appreciable amounts of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. These ions can react with soap to form insoluble deposits called scum. Such reactions reduce the soap available for cleaning.

Many synthetic detergents remain effective in hard water because they do not form the same insoluble calcium and magnesium salts as ordinary soap. This does not mean that every detergent is harmless or that all detergent formulations are suitable for every surface or purpose.

Cleaning, disinfection and antisepsis

These terms describe different activities:

  • Cleaning: Removes dirt, grease and many microorganisms from a surface, often using soap or detergent and water.
  • Disinfection: Uses an appropriate agent to kill or inactivate many disease-causing microorganisms on non-living surfaces.
  • Antisepsis: Uses a suitably formulated antimicrobial substance on living tissue, such as skin.

A detergent is not automatically a disinfectant. Likewise, a disinfectant intended for a household surface should not automatically be applied to human skin.

Important chemical safety rules

Household products must be used according to their labels and intended purposes. Many concentrated cleaning chemicals can irritate or damage skin and eyes.

Never mix household bleach with acids, including vinegar, or with ammonia-containing cleaners. Such mixtures can release dangerous gases. Different cleaning products should not be combined merely because each is useful when used separately.

All household chemicals should be stored in suitable, clearly identified containers and kept away from children. Food containers should not be reused to store hazardous cleaners.

Prelims focus

  • Common salt is NaCl.
  • Baking soda is NaHCO3; washing soda is Na2CO3·10H2O.
  • Vinegar contains dilute ethanoic acid.
  • Ordinary soap forms scum with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water.
  • Micelles help soap disperse grease in water.
  • Household liquid bleach commonly contains sodium hypochlorite.
  • Trap: Cleaning, disinfection and antisepsis are related but different processes.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 2, Acids, Bases and Salts, sections on common salt and chemicals derived from it, NCERT 2026–27 reprint consulted 3 November 2026. NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 4, Carbon and its Compounds, section on soaps and detergents, consulted through IIT Kanpur SATHEE on 3 November 2026. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Cleaning and Disinfecting with Bleach, 24 April 2024, and guidance distinguishing cleaning, sanitising and disinfecting, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Household Chemicals: Cleaning, Washing, Disinfection and Safety

body:
How are medicines classified?

A pharmaceutical is a medicinal product used to prevent, diagnose or treat disease, relieve symptoms or otherwise support health. Its active ingredient is the substance responsible for its intended medicinal effect.

Medicines are classified according to what they do. A single medicine can belong to more than 1 functional category. Understanding these categories prevents confusion between medicines that relieve symptoms and those that act on an underlying cause.

Common categories of medicines

CategoryMain actionExample
AnalgesicRelieves painParacetamol
AntipyreticReduces feverParacetamol
Anti-inflammatory medicineReduces inflammation and related symptomsIbuprofen
AntacidNeutralises excess stomach acidMagnesium hydroxide
AntibioticActs against susceptible bacteriaPenicillin-class antibiotics
AntisepticReduces or controls microorganisms on living tissueAppropriately formulated povidone-iodine

Paracetamol is both an analgesic and an antipyretic: it can relieve pain and reduce fever. However, reducing fever does not necessarily eliminate the infection or other condition causing the fever.

Antacids help neutralise stomach acid. For example, magnesium hydroxide is basic and can react with excess acid. This is an application of the school-level concept of acid-base neutralisation. An antacid treats acidity-related symptoms; it is not an antibiotic.

Why do antibiotics not treat viral infections?

Antibiotics act against bacteria through mechanisms that affect bacterial structures or processes. They do not treat ordinary viral infections such as the common cold or influenza. Antibiotics are therefore not a general treatment for every fever, cough or sore throat.

Unnecessary or incorrect antibiotic use can contribute to antimicrobial resistance, in which microorganisms become less susceptible to medicines that previously controlled them. Antibiotics should be used only when clinically appropriate and as prescribed.

Antibiotic is not another word for every antimicrobial medicine. Antimicrobials include drugs acting against bacteria, viruses, fungi and certain parasites. Antibiotics are specifically associated with bacterial infections.

Vaccines are different from antibiotics

Vaccines stimulate the immune system to recognise a particular infectious agent and help prevent disease or reduce its severity. They do not work in the same way as antibiotics, which act against susceptible bacteria.

Vaccination is primarily a preventive measure, although certain vaccines can also be given after an exposure as part of medical prevention. An antibiotic is not a substitute for vaccination, and vaccination is not a general treatment for an established bacterial infection.

Oral Rehydration Salts and dehydration

Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) provide glucose and electrolytes which, when dissolved in the prescribed amount of safe water, support the replacement of fluid and salts lost during diarrhoea.

ORS addresses dehydration. It is not an antibiotic and does not directly kill the microorganism responsible for an infection. A person with severe dehydration or serious symptoms may require urgent medical treatment.

Antiseptics and disinfectants are not interchangeable

Antiseptics are formulated for appropriate use on living tissue. Disinfectants are generally intended for non-living surfaces. For example, a suitable povidone-iodine preparation may be used as a skin antiseptic, whereas ordinary sodium-hypochlorite household bleach is intended for surfaces and must not be applied to wounds.

Why medicine names and doses matter

A medicine may have a generic name, identifying its active ingredient, and one or more brand names. The generic name helps identify what chemical or medicinal substance is present.

The dose is the quantity administered. A medicine is not harmless simply because it is commonly used. Excessive paracetamol, for example, can cause serious liver injury. The correct medicine, dose and duration depend on the patient's circumstances and professional guidance.

Connecting the useful chemicals in this lesson

The same basic chemistry helps explain several everyday sectors. Carbon-rich resources such as petroleum supply fuels and raw materials for polymers. Mineral resources such as limestone and silica are important for cement and glass. Plant nutrients are supplied through suitable fertilisers and manures. Household chemicals support cleaning and hygiene, while pharmaceutical substances have specific medical purposes.

The correct application depends on chemical composition and properties, not simply on whether a substance is natural, synthetic or widely used.

Prelims focus

  • Analgesics relieve pain; antipyretics reduce fever.
  • Paracetamol can act as both an analgesic and an antipyretic.
  • Antacids neutralise stomach acid.
  • Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria, not ordinary viral infections.
  • Vaccines stimulate immune protection; ORS replaces lost water and electrolytes.
  • Antiseptics are formulated for living tissue; disinfectants are generally used on non-living surfaces.
  • Trap: Relieving a symptom does not necessarily treat the underlying cause of an illness.

[World Health Organization, Antimicrobial Resistance, guidance current to July 2026; Vaccines and Immunization, introductory guidance; and Oral Rehydration Salts guidance, all consulted 3 November 2026. National Health Service, information on paracetamol and antacids, consulted 3 November 2026. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, antibiotic use guidance, consulted 3 November 2026. NCERT, Science, Class 7, ch. 5, Acids, Bases and Salts, printed pp. 49–56, 2018–19 edition.]

pictures.caption: Vaccines prepare immune protection; antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria.
